headline: A survey took the ten-year to 5.11%. An auction kept it there.
standfirst: Wednesday was the Treasury market's worst day since the April 2025 tariff shock, and it started with a purchasing managers' survey. S&P Global's flash composite PMI printed 58.4, the highest since July 2021, with input prices at their highest since October 2022; the ten-year yield rose 14.6bp to 5.116%, its highest close since July 2007, the two-year 12.8bp to 4.903%, and the five-year closed above 5% for the first time since 2007. Then Treasury's $70 billion five-year auction stopped at 5.033%, the highest since June 2006, 3bp cheap to the market, with dealers left holding the most paper since 2024. Fed Governor Barr said further hikes are “likely needed” and October went to 73% priced. Stocks fell — the S&P 500 0.75% to 7,706.03, the Nasdaq 1.13% off its record, the Russell 2000 1.77% — with energy the only sector up, because Brent rose 3.86% back above $100 after Iran's president said the strait stays shut. Today: the SNB at 03:30 ET, claims and three Fed speakers before the open, a $44 billion seven-year at 13:00, and Xi in the Oval Office.

bullets.title: The PMI said the economy is running at 5%. The Fed had just hiked into that.
bullets.text: The flash composite rose to 58.4 from 56.0 against 55.3 expected — a fourth straight monthly rise and the fastest since July 2021. Services printed 58.7, a 59-month high; manufacturing 57.0, a 52-month high, after the New York, Philadelphia and Richmond Fed surveys had all fallen this month. New orders rose to 58.2, the strongest since March 2022; backlogs are the highest since May 2022; supplier delivery delays are the widest since July 2022; and the input-price index jumped to 66.4 from 59.9, the highest since October 2022, on fuel, diesel, wages and materials. S&P Global's Chris Williamson put the survey at about 5% annualised growth, with 4% signalled for the third quarter; the Atlanta Fed's tracker is at 5.1%. The Atlanta Fed's own one-year business inflation expectation rose to 2.4% from 2.2%. Europe printed strong too: the euro-area composite 53.1 against 51.5, German services 52.9 after five months of contraction; only the UK softened, its composite slipping to 51.7.

bullets.title: Then the five-year auction tailed, and the belly of the curve went through 5%
bullets.text: The $70 billion five-year stopped at 5.033% against 4.393% in August — the highest since June 2006 and about 3bp above the 5.002% the issue was trading at the deadline. Bid-to-cover was 2.21 against a 2.33 six-auction average; indirects took 54.31%; primary dealers were left with 15.8%, the largest share since 2024. Yields rose further after the result. The ten-year closed at 5.116%, up 14.6bp, its largest one-day rise since 7 April 2025 and a move Sina's desk note called roughly four standard deviations, two weeks after a three-sigma day; the two-year at 4.903% is the highest since May 2024 and the thirty-year at 5.402% since June 2007. Swaps now fully price three quarter-point hikes over the next year with hedging for a fourth, which would take the funds rate to 5%. The MOVE index closed at its highest since March. Treasury buys back up to $6 billion of 20- to 30-year paper today, and sells $44 billion of seven-years at 13:00 ET; the last stop was 4.512%. The 30-year mortgage rate is 7.12%, the highest since May 2024.

bullets.title: Barr is a voter, and he said the Fed was “out of position”
bullets.text: Governor Michael Barr, in remarks to a housing conference in Chicago, said “further policy adjustments are likely to be needed” to return inflation to 2% in a timely way, that the committee had been “out of position” and had “made an adjustment in the right direction”, and that risks to inflation have risen while risks to the labour market have receded. Unlike Barkin, Collins, Goolsbee and Musalem earlier in the week, Barr votes. The CME's FedWatch put a hike at the 27–28 October meeting at 73%, from 48.7% a week ago; December is now the second hike, not the first. Sixteen of eighteen officials projected at least one more increase this year. The dollar index closed at 101.23, an eight-week high, the euro traded below 1.14 and sterling below 1.33; the Australian dollar was the weakest major even before this morning's jobs print of +39,500 against 20,000 expected.

bullets.title: Oil reversed six days on a speech and a struck ship — and the inventories said sell
bullets.text: Brent settled at $103.08, up $3.83 or 3.86%, and WTI's November contract at $92.16, up 1.81%, ending five sessions of declines. Iranian President Pezeshkian told the UN that Iran will not surrender and officials said the Strait of Hormuz stays closed until its conditions are met; a cargo vessel struck by an unidentified projectile caught fire inside the strait, killing two, according to UKMTO. Tanker tracking had three merchant ships through Hormuz on Tuesday against a ten-day average of about 15; Bank of America now puts the disruption at 4–8 million barrels a day and says $150 is possible if supply tightens further, while forecasting $80 for 2027. Aramco is offering Asian refiners more crude from outside the strait and has told European buyers there will be no October allocation. Against all of that, the EIA reported a 3.0 million barrel commercial build against a 0.7 million draw expected, and the market bought crude anyway. Trump still describes the talks as “very productive” and still puts a deal after the 3 November midterms.

bullets.title: Xi is in Washington, the truce is extended, and the tape did not care
bullets.text: Trump met Xi on the tarmac at Andrews on Wednesday evening — the first time a US president has done so since Obama met the Pope in 2015 — and Xi arrived saying the two countries should be “partners, not rivals”. Bessent said the trade truce that was due to expire on 10 November has been extended by two months. The bilateral is today, followed by a state dinner attended by Bezos, Musk, Pichai, Huang, Altman, Cook and the chief executives of GM and Stellantis; the agenda is AI, export controls, rare earths, Taiwan and Iran, and the expectation on both sides is pageantry over deliverables. None of it helped equities: Alphabet fell 3.58%, Amazon 2.24%, Nvidia 1.47% and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index 1.23%, while Meta rose 1.02%. Every sector but energy fell; utilities lost 1.92%, real estate 1.55%, consumer discretionary 1.50%. Overnight Tokyo reopened after three days and the Nikkei rose 1.65%; the Kospi added 0.9%; Hong Kong fell 0.75% and Shanghai 1%.

calendar.note: Expected to hold at zero. The franc is the currency that has not weakened against the dollar this month, so the pressure on the SNB is the opposite of everyone else's.
Three speakers around the claims print, the morning after a Governor said more hikes are likely needed. Williams gave no guidance on Tuesday; whether he does today is the tell.
Claims seen 201,000 after 196,000. With the PMI employment index at its strongest since June 2022, a sub-200,000 print would confirm the survey rather than surprise.
Seen at 620,000 after 607,000, following a 10.5% fall. Mortgage rates are 7.12%, and KB Home said on Tuesday that volumes, not prices, are what 7% does.

calendar.event: $44bn seven-year auction; Treasury buyback of up to $6bn
calendar.note: The last seven-year stopped at 4.512%; the yield is 5.05%. After the five-year tailed 3bp with dealers stuck holding 15.8%, this is the event of the day. The buyback is in 20- to 30-year paper, which is not where the auction is.

calendar.event: Trump–Xi bilateral at the White House; state dinner this evening
calendar.note: The truce extension is already announced. Anything on AI cooperation, rare earths or export controls trades semiconductors first; anything on Iran trades crude.

calendar.event: Durable goods (August); Michigan final 10:00; Fed's Williams 05:15
calendar.note: Durable goods seen −0.4% after +1.1%, ex-transport +0.6%, core capital goods +0.5%. Michigan sentiment 47.6; the one-year inflation expectation at 4.6% is the number.
About 90% priced for a hike from 4.35% after August jobs printed +39,500 against 20,000 expected, even with unemployment ticking up to 4.6%.

sessionNote: The overnight tape has held Wednesday rather than extended it. Brent is $103.21 and WTI $92.11, both within a tenth of a percent of the settle; the dollar index is 101.2; gold is unchanged at $4,319.70 and down 2.38% on the week; Bitcoin is $84,173, off 0.23%, having sat out the sell-off. Asia is split — Tokyo up 1.65% on reopening, Seoul up 0.9%, Hong Kong and Shanghai down — and the Australian dollar weakened into a strong jobs print. The day has a clear shape: the SNB before Europe opens, claims and three Fed speakers before New York, then a seven-year auction at 13:00 into a belly that just repriced 15bp, with Xi in the Oval Office at the same time. The US morning is the window. The auction is the event, and the tail is the number.
watchOut: Fading Wednesday because “it was only a survey”. The PMI started it, but the bond market did not sell off 15bp on a diffusion index alone: the five-year auction tailed with dealers forced to hold 15.8%, the MOVE index is at March highs, Treasury's $6 billion buyback is set against $114 billion of coupon supply this week, and a four-sigma day two weeks after a three-sigma day is a value-at-risk event — risk books shrink mechanically, and mechanical selling does not read your view. The second trap is the one flagged yesterday: six days of oil de-escalation reversed on one speech and one struck ship, exactly the asymmetry a $10 decline on pipeline tests and a tanker count implied. A long duration or short energy position sized for the trend is sized for the wrong week.

archive.headline: The Fed said “we’ll see”. The two-year auction said 4.787%.
archive.summary: Treasury sold $69 billion of two-years at 4.787%, the highest stop since May 2024, on demand that held; Brent settled at $99.25 for its first close under $100 since 9 September; four Fed officials, none voting this year, all leaned toward more. The Nasdaq closed at a second straight record while financials fell 1.97%.

archive.headline: An App Store ranking moved a trillion dollars
archive.summary: Meta's Muse agent topped the US iPhone chart and the CPU complex repriced around it: Meta +11.43%, AMD +9.95% to a first $1 trillion close, Intel +12%, Arm +17%, and the Nasdaq to its first record since June. Crude fell to an eleven-day low on Hormuz shipping data and the ten-year came back under 5%, into a $69 billion two-year auction.

archive.headline: The war premium leaks out before the UN
archive.summary: Monday with no US data and a live diplomatic wire. Crude fell for a fourth session as traders priced a chance of US–Iran contact at the UN General Assembly and Saudi Arabia worked to restore its East–West pipeline, with the ten-year coming into the day at 5.01% after its first close above 5% since July 2007.

archive.headline: The hike landed. The bond market blinked first.
archive.summary: Weekend edition. The Fed's unanimous 25bp on Wednesday took the Dow down 631 points and Thursday gave most of it back, with the S&P up 1.14% to 7,637.76 as the ten-year fell to 4.93% and oil slid. The weekend risk was the Iran war, with Trump saying he was near a decision on resuming large-scale strikes.

archive.headline: The ten-year touched 5% into the decision. The hike is not the event.
archive.summary: FOMC day. The 10-year had closed at 5.00% after touching 5.04%, the highest since 2007, with a 25bp hike priced at 92–94%. WTI had jumped 5.1% to $106.56 as fighting intensified in the Middle East; every US sector but energy closed red on Tuesday.

archive.headline: Core CPI ran hot into an FOMC that is now 90% priced to hike
archive.summary: Weekend edition. Core CPI rose 0.3% on the month against 0.2% expected, PPI came in at 5.4% year-over-year, and September hike odds moved from 61% to about 90%. Equities closed the week higher regardless — S&P +0.86% Friday, VIX −11% — while the 10-year finished at 4.96%.

archive.headline: Core CPI at a four-month high, hike odds jump to ~90%
archive.summary: Headline CPI held at 3.4% year-over-year but core rose 0.3% on the month against 0.2% expected. Energy added 2.1% and gasoline 3.9%; airline fares rose 2.7%. Equities rallied regardless — S&P +0.86%, VIX −11% — while the 10-year touched 4.97%.
